A.trap: Room number used as an identifier
A.fix: Use two person-specific identifiers (name + DOB or MRN). Rooms and beds are locations, not identifiers.
Implied = emergency/unconscious or patient cooperates with a routine procedure. Informed = risks, benefits and alternatives explained, usually written, for stress tests and invasive tests.
Airborne (TB, measles, varicella): N95 + negative-pressure room. Droplet (influenza, pertussis): surgical mask within about 6 ft. Contact (MRSA, C. diff): gown + gloves.
Spores are not reliably killed by alcohol — wash with soap and water.
Clip excess hair; razors cause nicks. Clean oils, lightly abrade, let the skin dry.

A.trap: Using family or children to interpret
A.fix: Use a qualified medical interpreter. Minors only in an emergency.
Technicians do not interpret. "Your doctor will review it with you."
A competent adult may refuse any test. Stop, explain, notify the nurse/provider, document.

A.trap: Leaving a deteriorating patient to get help
A.fix: Stay with the patient, keep them safe and call for help.
CDC example: gloves → goggles/face shield → gown → mask/respirator, then hand hygiene. Donning is the reverse: gown → mask → goggles → gloves.

B.trap: V1 and V2 swapped or too high
B.fix: V1 = 4th ICS RIGHT sternal border, V2 = 4th ICS LEFT. Find the angle of Louis (2nd rib) and count down. High placement mimics RBBB/septal changes.
V4 = 5th ICS, midclavicular line. In women place it under the breast, not on breast tissue.

B.trap: RA–LA vs RA–RL vs LA–LL reversal
B.fix: RA–LA: lead I inverted, aVR upright. RA–RL: lead II nearly flat. LA–LL: subtle, lead III inverted, P taller in I than II. RL–LL: almost no change.
AHA: RA white, LA black, LL red, RL green ("white on the right, smoke over fire"). IEC: RA red, LA yellow, LL green, RL black.
Tremor: irregular, varies, from muscle tension or cold. 60-cycle: perfectly regular fine fuzz from electrical devices.

B.trap: Half standard vs double paper speed
B.fix: Gain changes HEIGHT (5 mm pulse = half standard). Paper speed changes WIDTH (50 mm/s doubles widths).
Diagnostic: 0.05 Hz low cut, ≥150 Hz high cut (adults). Monitor filters can distort the ST segment.
RV infarct: move chest leads to the right only. Dextrocardia: right-sided chest leads AND reverse the arm electrodes.
V7–V9 stay on the same horizontal line as V6 (posterior axillary, mid-scapular, paraspinal).
I, II, III are bipolar. aVR, aVL, aVF are augmented unipolar. Lead I + Lead III = Lead II (Einthoven).

C.fix: Left Axis Deviation (I up, aVF down, II down) vs Left Anterior Descending artery (V1–V4). Read the context.
I SAW LA: Inferior II/III/aVF, Septal V1–V2, Anterior V3–V4, Lateral I/aVL/V5–V6.
RCA → inferior (+ RV, SA/AV nodes). LAD → septal/anterior. Circumflex → lateral. Posterior → mirror changes in V1–V3.
ST depression opposite the injured wall (e.g., aVL in inferior MI) supports STEMI; it is not a second infarct.
ST depression + tall R in V1–V3 → think posterior; confirm with V7–V9.
Pericarditis: diffuse ST elevation + PR depression, no territory, no reciprocal change (except aVR/V1).
Discordant ST-T in LBBB is expected. Concordant changes are worrying.
Small q < 0.04 s in I, aVL, V5–V6 is normal. Pathologic Q ≥ 0.04 s or ≥ 25% of R height.
Pulmonale (lungs → right atrium): tall, peaked ≥ 2.5 mm. Mitrale (left atrium): wide ≥ 0.12 s, notched.
High K: narrow, tented T in many leads. Hyperacute T: broad, bulky, in one territory.
High K → peaked T; low K → U waves. High Ca → short QT; low Ca → long QT.
RBBB, RVH, posterior MI (also WPW, normal in children). LBBB gives a deep QS in V1.
Women ≥ 1.5 mm, men ≥ 40 ≥ 2 mm, men < 40 ≥ 2.5 mm; all other leads ≥ 1 mm in two contiguous leads.

D.fix: Bruce stage 1: 1.7 mph, 10%. Modified Bruce adds 1.7 mph at 0% and 5% first. Each stage is 3 minutes.
Systolic rises with work; diastolic stays the same or falls slightly. A falling systolic BP with increasing work is a stop sign.
Symptomatic severe AS = absolute; asymptomatic severe AS = relative. Acute MI within 2 days = absolute.
≥ 1 mm horizontal or downsloping depression ~80 ms after J point. Rapid upsloping is usually normal.
Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors → hold at least 12 hours.
Tight grip overestimates METs and adds artifact.
Absolute indication to stop the test.

E.fix: Holter records continuously (24–48 h); the button only marks symptoms. Event recorders save when activated (loop recorders also keep pre-event memory).
Time + symptom + activity is what makes the recording useful.
Check the patient first; a loose lead can mimic asystole.
Holter electrodes go over bone (sternum/ribs) to reduce motion artifact.
Standard Holter recorders must stay dry; follow the device instructions for patches.

F.fix: AF: no P waves, irregularly irregular. MAT: ≥ 3 P shapes, rate > 100. Flutter: regular sawtooth waves.
A regular narrow rhythm at ~150 → hunt for hidden flutter waves.
Mobitz I: PR grows then drops. Mobitz II: PR constant then drops (dangerous). 2:1 cannot be typed from one strip.
Third degree: P waves march through, PR varies randomly, R–R regular.
Arrhythmia: gradual, with breathing. Arrest: abrupt missing beat, pause not a multiple of P–P.
PAC: early abnormal upright P, narrow QRS. PJC: inverted/absent P. PVC: wide, no P, compensatory pause.
Bigeminy every 2nd beat, trigeminy every 3rd. Couplet = 2 PVCs in a row; 3+ = VT run.

F.trap: Failure to capture vs failure to sense
F.fix: Capture: spike, no response. Sense: spikes ignore the patient's own beats.

F.trap: Fine VF vs asystole vs loose lead
F.fix: Confirm in two leads, check gain and connections, CHECK THE PATIENT.
1500 ÷ SMALL boxes, 300 ÷ LARGE boxes — regular rhythms only. Irregular → 6-second × 10.
QT ÷ √RR (RR in seconds). Don't forget the square root.
Scooped ST = effect. New arrhythmias, nausea, visual changes = toxicity.
VF and pulseless VT are shocked. Asystole and PEA are not.
Beta blocker / ACE inhibitor / ARB / dihydropyridine CCB (little AV effect).
